THE EFFECTS OF LIGHTING COLOR TEMPERATURE ON TEACHER SELF-EFFICACY
By
ALYSSA OATES
Bachelor of Science in Human Sciences
Oklahoma State University
Stillwater, Oklahoma
2023
Submitted to the Faculty of the
Graduate College of the
Oklahoma State University
in partial fulfillment of
the requirements for
the Degree of
MASTER OF SCIENCE
May, 2024

Name: ALYSSA OATES
Date of Degree: MAY 2024
Title of Study: THE EFFECTS OF LIGHTING COLOR TEMPERATURE ON TEACHER
SELF-EFFICACY
Major Field: DESIGN, HOUSING, AND MERCHANDISING
Abstract:
Classroom design has been a research topic of interest for decades and has become more
and more popular over the last several years. Researchers have developed new methods for
studying and quantifying the effects of classroom design on students and their behavior. While
this information has been beneficial, teachers have been largely left out of this conversation.
Educators have an incredible impact on their students and therefore should be included in these
studies to better understand how the classroom environment impacts them. Similarly, studies
about lighting color temperature in the classroom environment are limited. Classroom and
educational design is heavily based on evidence-based design, therefore literature that considers
the viewpoints of educators and students are crucial to designing environments that benefit the
users, There is a critical need to ensure that educators can carry out their respected roles in an
environment in which the lighting positively impacts their self-efficacy and desire to be present
in the classroom. The purpose of this study was to assess if the integration of cool tone lighting
in a virtual simulation of an early childhood classroom improves cognitive and physiological
measurements in educators. The specific aims of the study include the following: a) Determine if
the addition of cool tone lighting in the virtual early childhood education classroom will result in
a reduction in cognitive load, as compared to the warm tone lighting; b) Determine if the
addition of cool tone lighting in the virtual early childhood education classroom will result in a
reduction in physiological measurements, as compared to the warm tone lighting; c) Determine
how the educator’s cognitive load affects their self-efficacy; d) Determine how the educator’s
physiological measurements affect their satisfaction and intent to spend time in the classroom
environment. 30 participants were recruited to experience two virtual classroom environments
with different lighting correlated color temperatures (CCTs). Participants answered survey
questions related to their perceived cognitive load, self-efficacy, and emotions experienced while
in each of the classrooms. The study found that there were significant differences in perceived
cognitive load, self-efficacy, and emotions between the warm-tone and cool-tone lighting
environments. The study also found correlations between cognitive load and self-efficacy. The
findings suggest that lighting CCT does impact educators and their ability to succeed in the
classroom. There are important implications for the design of classrooms to improve the
wellbeing and success of educators.

CHAPTER ONE
INTRODUCTION
I. INTRODUCTION
The brain is the most complex organ in the human body, it is constantly changing and
growing. The early childhood stage of life is when the brain changes and grows the most rapidly,
making this stage critical (Britto et al., 2017). The early childhood stage determines various
factors later in a person’s life, such as their ability to learn, their health and wellbeing, and even
their career (Tierney & Nelson III, 2009; Britto et al., 2017). The school classroom plays an
extensive role in the development of humans, as they spend a majority of their first eighteen
years in these settings. There is an abundance of research already existing about the school
environment and its impacts on human development and wellbeing. One area of research that has
been heavily explored is the Montessori Classroom (Fisher et al., 2014). The Montessori
classroom concept is used around the world and has inspired other research topics regarding
learning environments, such as the classroom, and its effect on students. Research studying the
effect of wall decorations and object placement on cooperation in young children has been
carried out (Kuh, 2014). Researchers have also turned to the classroom environment to
1

understand its effects on child engagement. A main focus has been put on to lighting in the
classroom, specifically the type of lighting (LED vs. fluorescent) and what effect it has on
student engagement (Pulay & Williamson, 2019). Color temperature of lighting in the classroom
has been briefly explored, but results are not in-depth and are not specifically applied to teacher
self-efficacy.
Students are not the only users being affected by the classroom environment; educators also
spend the majority of their day within one classroom. Teaching can be stress inducing, which can
then impact their performance. The educator’s ability to effectively teach materials to students is
imperative, especially during the early childhood phase of life due to the fact that children’s
brains are rapidly developing during this time. Educators’ stressors can come from a multitude of
variables; some common stressors noted in Richards’ (2012) article include student behavior
problems, a feeling of isolation or inferiority, and a lack of control. These stressors will be
discussed more in depth in chapter two.
Classrooms and other learning environments are functional spaces that require attention to
detail to properly ensure its compatibility with the end-users. There is an opportunity to provide
additional aesthetic value to the space in order to increase the happiness, comfort, and
engagement of the users of the space. Often in preschool or early childhood education settings,
teachers and students spend the majority of their day in one classroom. Because of the extensive
time spent in these settings, it is important for the space to provide functional and aesthetic value
in order to maximize positive relations for all end-users. By introducing various lighting
solutions into an early childhood education classroom, we can improve the overall satisfaction of
educators and reduce their cognitive load. The first chapter of this thesis presents the background
of the study, it states the problem of the study and describes its significance, and it presents a
2

brief overview of the methodology used. The chapter concludes by pointing out and defining key
terms used throughout the writing.
II. THE BACKGROUND OF THE STUDY
The following section provides a discussion on benefits provided by natural lighting, teacher
burnout, and the effects on their performance and student engagement. Natural daylight provides
many physical and psychological benefits for the human body, including the ability to improve
mood and brain activity, and decrease stress and violent behavior (Shishegar & Boubekri, 2016).
Natural daylight is also very beneficial in school settings and has been shown to enhance
students’ learning capabilities and improve their mood, among other benefits (Shishegar &
Boubekri, 2016; Heschong & Mahone, 2003; Küller & Lindsten, 1992). Barrett et al. (2015)
even claims that natural light should be the main source of lighting in schools, except for when
daylight fades. While natural lighting has many benefits for students and educators alike, it may
not always be an option. Many schools in the United States have classrooms without a source for
natural light; according to Alexander & Lewis (2014), approximately 69% of elementary schools
do not have windows in the classrooms. Natural daylight is essential in order to make sure
students are learning in a healthy and stimulating environment. While adding windows or
skylights may not be an option for some schools, changing the artificial lighting in the
classrooms can be done.
Both artificial and natural lighting have the capabilities of impacting students’ ability to
perform well on academic tests (Tanner, 2009). Natural lighting also has the ability to enhance a
student’s physical and psychological health (Shishegar & Boubekri, 2016; Heschong & Mahone,
2003; Küller & Lindsten, 1992). Lighting plays various roles in our daily lives, but its main
function is to provide visual information and allow us to visualize tasks, colors, textures, etc. It
3

can impact our levels of alertness, our mental focus capabilities, and our cognitive performance
(Vandewalle, 2009). Lighting systems that mimic the patterns of the sun are called circadian
lighting systems. These systems change the color temperature of lighting throughout the day to
match the color temperature of the sun at that time. Using these types of systems can positively
affect productivity levels, health, and alertness. However, these systems can be expensive for
most schools; for schools without windows that cannot afford a complex lighting system like
circadian lighting, what lighting designs can be used to positively impact the students and
educators?
According to a 2008 study, lighting was shown to be a significant factor for the satisfaction
of educators (Ruszala, 2008). With teacher burnout increasing due to COVID-19, teacher
shortages, and student misbehavior in the classroom, it is important that we understand how the
educator plays a role in the students’ ability to learn and what role lighting plays in that dynamic.
According to two different studies, an educator’s burnout can lead to a decrease in their teaching
efficiency (Shen et al., 2015; Whipp et al., 2007). Furthermore, this decrease in efficiency can
have an impact on the levels of motivation and engagement of the students. Teacher burnout can
occur for a multitude of reasons, and will greatly depend on the educator and their circumstances
and environment. However, according to Ghanizadeh and Jahedizadeh (2015), teacher burnout
can be attributed to self-efficacy, self-esteem, pedagogical barriers, among others. The same
researchers found that the consequences of burnout, specifically related to the educator, can be a
reduction in their self-efficacy. If a teacher does not feel confident enough in their teaching
methods, then the students will not receive the highest quality of education that they need. The
design of classrooms has an opportunity to provide an environment that will positively impact
the educator, who can then focus on educating their students. A teacher’s work environment is a
4

student’s learning environment. We cannot focus on one or the other, they interact on a daily
basis, therefore we must consider all users of the space when designing classrooms that will
impact the success of those who use it.
III. THE NEED FOR THE STUDY
The long-term goal of this proposed research study was to develop an understanding of the
role in which the classroom environment plays in the educator’s ability to perform well while
teaching. The primary objective of this study was to assess if the integration of cool tone lighting
in a virtual simulation of an early childhood classroom improves cognitive and physiological
measurements in educators. The rationale for this study was that the development of a new
lighting design for early childhood education classrooms will improve the educator’s perceived
ability to effectively teach the necessary materials to students.
It was the expectation that the successful completion of this study would show that
classrooms designed with cool tone lighting systems would result in an improvement of stress
levels and general cognitive and physiological measurements in educators when compared to a
classroom with warm tone or white lighting. It was expected that educators would experience a
reduction in stress levels (see page 41 for instruments). The findings from this study have the
potential to significantly impact the self-efficacy of educators, which will have a positive impact
on their careers and the success of their students. The early childhood stage of life is filled with
critical milestones that will prepare the children for adolescence and adulthood. Their brains are
rapidly forming and changing to accommodate for the new information they learn every day.
Because of this, it is important to make sure learning environments provide the necessary tools
for this rapid learning and development. Due to the aforementioned factors, there is a critical
need to ensure that educators can carry out their respected roles in an environment which
5

positively impacts their self-efficacy and desire to be present in the classroom. Without this type
of environment, children may not receive the interactions or learning tools that encourage them
to properly integrate into society, which can negatively affect them later in life.
IV. SPECIFIC AIMS
The aims of the study were divided into four sections in order to study the distinct aspects of
the educators’ cognitive and physiological measurements, as they relate to the scope of the study.
§ Specific Aim 1
Determine if the addition of cool tone lighting in the virtual early childhood education
classroom will result in a reduction in cognitive load, as compared to the warm tone lighting.
§ Specific Aim 2
Determine if the addition of cool tone lighting in the virtual early childhood education
classroom will result in a reduction in physiological measurements, as compared to the warm
tone lighting.
§ Specific Aim 3
Determine how the educator’s cognitive load affects their self-efficacy.
§ Specific Aim 4
Determine how the educator’s physiological measurements affect their satisfaction and intent
to spend time in the classroom environment.
V. RESEARCH QUESTIONS
1. How does the color temperature of the lighting affect cognitive load while in the
environment? (H1)
2. How does the color temperature of the lighting affect physiological measurements
while in the environment? (H2)
6

3. How does the educator’s cognitive load affect their self-efficacy? (H3)
4. How does the educator’s physiological measurements affect their satisfaction and
intent to spend time in the classroom environment? (H4)

VII. THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY
The early childhood stage of life is a time of rapid development in the brain, making this a
crucial time period in the classroom environment. Many studies revolving around classroom
design focus on elementary, middle, or high schools. Early childhood education centers are often
overlooked despite their importance. Interior designers offer a unique perspective to the design
of these environments as they are taught how spaces impact the health, safety, and wellbeing of
the users. Designers also consider interactions between users and how those will shape the
overall design of the space. As there are limited data supporting lighting color temperature
choices in early child education classrooms, studies in this area are vital to the development of
both the education design field and designers’ understanding of the implications of evidence-
based design.
VIII. OVERVIEW OF METHODOLOGY
This research study aimed to determine if cool tone lighting in an early childhood education
classroom could aid in improving physiological and cognitive measures, ultimately deciding the
impact on teacher self-efficacy. For this study, participants observed and interacted with two
different, but similar virtual classroom environments to determine the effects of cool tone
lighting on their self-efficacy, cognitive load, and physiological measurements. The virtual
environments were designed in Revit and SketchUp and measured the perceptions of the space
and the participants’ physiological, cognitive, and emotional responses to virtual classrooms with
warm tone or cool tone lighting. Both of the environments utilized design techniques that are
similar to those used within the education design field. The classroom design was modeled after
an existing classroom in a child development lab on the campus of a midwestern university.
8

For this study, participants started by entering a neutral virtual environment in order to allow
them to understand the virtual reality equipment (controls, headset, etc.) before they entered into
one of the two virtual classroom environments that was randomly selected ahead of time. In the
traditional environment, warm tone lighting with a color temperature of 3,000K was utilized. The
redesigned environment is the same classroom as the traditional environment, except the lighting
color temperature was 4,100K (cool tone). These color temperatures were chosen based off of
past research studies conducted (Pulay et al., 2018). Participants entered both spaces using a
virtual reality headset and used the handsets to move around the space. During this virtual
experience, participants were asked to complete a lesson plan, which will be further discussed in
Chapter Three. Quantitative data was collected through the participant’s heart rate and survey
results. More information on the study methods will be provided in Chapter Three of this thesis.
IX. SCOPE OF THE RESEARCH
The research study discusses the redesign of lighting systems in early childhood education
classrooms by replacing warm tone lighting with cool tone lighting. By redesigning these
lighting systems, it can be used as a precedent for future early childhood education classroom
designs. This research did not aim to study the other design features of classrooms such as color,
room layout, technology, etc.; this research was strictly concerned with lighting design. Any
other design variables or interior spaces of schools were beyond the scope of this study. This
study was also limited to the perspective of the educator; students were not recruited for their
input.
X. PROBLEM STATEMENT
Educators experience a lot of stress while in classroom environments due to many different
factors. The stress can lead to a decline in self-efficacy, which can negatively impact the
9

engagement and academic success of students. There was an opportunity to reduce stress and
improve engagement through design interventions. Design interventions such as incorporating
cool tone lighting designs could be more beneficial for both the educators and students that use
these spaces daily.
XI. DEFINITIONS OF TERMS
Correlated Color Temperature (CCT): Measured in Kelvin (K), color temperature refers to
the color of a light. E.g. 1,000K is a very warm tone light, 5,000K simulates daylight or a neutral
white light, 10,000K is a very cool tone light.
Early Childhood: This stage in life is commonly considered to encompass children between
birth and eight years old. This stage is filled with many milestones.
Evidence-Based Design: The deliberate process of using evidence from research and literature
to make design decisions with the goal of maximizing the end-users health, safety, and welfare.
Negative Engagement: Engagement that is defined by a lack of motivation, lack of intent to
succeed, conflicts, and dysregulation (Vitiello et al., 2012).
Pedagogy: The science of teaching; the methods utilized by educator’s to teach their students
material (Merriam-Webster, n.d.).
Positive Engagement: Engagement that is defined by students being motivated, confident, and
having an intent to succeed on their tasks (Vitiello et al., 2012).
Self-Efficacy: A person’s belief that they are capable of learning or performing tasks;
hypothesized to impact choices, effort, and achievement levels (Bandura, 1997).
10

CHAPTER TWO
LITERATURE REVIEW
I. INTRODUCTION
The following section provides a review of literature pertaining to classroom design, early
childhood, and engagement, and how they interact and relate to one another in educational
settings. By considering all of these components in the design of classrooms, designers have the
ability to create a space that supports and encourages the well-being and development of youth.
II. THE EDUCATOR AND SELF-EFFICACY
Over the course of eleven years, the percentage of teacher’s affected by teacher burnout
nearly doubled from 30% to 57.77% (Blazer, 2010; Trinidad, 2021). With that dramatic increase,
likely caused by a number of factors revolving the COVID-19 pandemic, it is important that we
understand the effects of teacher burnout and what effect it will specifically have on student
engagement and the overall teaching quality of educators. According to several studies, teacher
burnout can have a negative impact on their quality of life and can lead to a deterioration in their
teaching efficiency (Shen et al., 2015; Whipp et al., 2007). These qualities may cause an increase
11

in teacher absenteeism, which in turn will have a negative impact on their productivity levels.
However, teacher burnout does not just have a negative impact on the educator. Burnout can lead
to a decrease in a student’s desire to be involved in the school work and activities, and can lead
to an overall decrease in motivation levels (Ghanizadeh & Jahedizadeh, 2015). With this
information, it is important to consider that the teacher’s working environment is the student’s
learning environment. It is irresponsible to focus on just one of the two parties involved; teachers
and students interact in classrooms on a daily basis, their environment needs to work for both of
them. If the environment is efficient and effective, then both the educators and students can
perform their roles to the best of their abilities.
When discussing teacher burnout, it should be noted that emotional exhaustion is reported to
be the central quality, and it often represents feelings of being emotionally overextended and
exhausted (Maslach et al., 2001). With emotional exhaustion being the central quality, and most
widely reported cause of burnout, it is important to understand the ramifications of it. Emotional
exhaustion has discouraged teachers from understanding the quality of the tasks and materials
they taught or the methods they utilized in the classroom (Shen et al., 2015). Being emotionally
overextended and exhausted can also lead educator’s to be impatient with students when
teaching new material (Shen et al., 2015). When exhausted, teachers can show that through their
attitude towards students; they may be more aggressive or visibly upset towards students, which
can negatively affect their desire to be present and engaged. Educator’s being impatient with
their students may include examples of them not providing in-depth explanations or examples of
material, which can negatively impact the student’s ability to be successful. Once passionate
about teaching, burnout can cause educator’s to lose their passion and turn towards other career
opportunities, often outside of the education field.
12

When discussing emotional exhaustion, it is important to note that an educator’s self-efficacy
may suffer if they are experiencing exhaustion, causing them to doubt themselves and their
skills. When referring to efficacy, there are three main types that are widely accepted: general,
personal, and collective. General efficacy is noted to be the extent to which an educator believes
their students are capable of learning the material that is being taught (Charles, 2017). General
efficacy is more concerned with the material being taught in class and its difficulty level in
relation to the academic level of the students. Personal efficacy, or sometimes referred to as self-
efficacy, is the extent to which an educator believes their students can learn under their personal
instruction methods (Charles, 2017). This type of efficacy is concerned with the educator’s
pedagogy and how they feel their students will succeed under their instruction. Personal efficacy
is one of the potential effects of emotional exhaustion, as teachers may begin to doubt their
ability to properly and effectively teach their students. The third major type of efficacy is
collective efficacy. This type refers to the beliefs of groups of teachers that they are able to work
together as a team to make a positive impact on their students (Charles, 2017). Collective
efficacy is largely affected by the individual teacher’s personal efficacy, if one or more teachers
in a group begin to experience self-doubt, that feeling can translate to the other teachers.
An educator’s self-efficacy has been noted to have an important role in the psychological and
physical health of the individual (Bal-Taştan et al., 2018). The educator’s self-efficacy also has
an effect on those that are around them; their efficacy can make their environment seem positive
or negative. According to Porter and Brophy (1988), a teacher that is confident in themselves and
their teaching pedagogy is more likely to provide an environment that is more efficient and
conducive to learning and engaged behavior. Educators have a very important role in the
classroom of providing an environment that will engage the students, and ultimately, prepare
13

them for later academic levels and success. If the students are to succeed under the leadership of
a teacher, the teacher needs to be able to be confident in their pedagogy in order to effectively
communicate and educate the students. Having a high self-efficacy can lead to positive teaching
behaviors, directly strengthening student achievement; this is mainly due to teachers with high
self-efficacy using more open-ended questions, having more interactive learning opportunities,
more group learning activities, etc. (Gavora, 2010). Instead of defaulting to a lecture mode of
teaching and not providing opportunities for questions or interactive learning, teacher’s with high
self-efficacy tend to be more flexible and innovative with their teaching methods, which can be
beneficial to students with various learning styles. Overall, an educator’s self-efficacy beliefs can
be noted to relate with more effective teaching practices and the academic performance levels of
their students.
III. EARLY CHILDHOOD LIFE STAGE
The early childhood stage of life is commonly considered to include children from birth to
the age of eight years; however, the main group of children to utilize early childhood care
facilities are pre-school age which includes children between the ages of two and six (Essa &
Burnham, 2019). Although this stage only lasts eight years, there are many milestones that
happen for children during this period. For the scope of this study, we will focus on children
between the ages of two and six years, as those are the children commonly using the proposed
facilities.
Two-year-olds are in a transitional stage of life, moving from babyhood to childhood. This
year is characterized by a child gaining control of their body, increasing control of their fingers,
and widening their vocabulary (Essa & Burnham, 2019). Generally, children of this age do not
cooperate or share with others, they express their growing sense of independence by taking
14

objects from others and throwing tantrums (Essa & Burnham, 2019). At three years old, children
start to be more social and play or do activities together and side-by-side. Their social problem-
solving skills are becoming apparent, but will need lots of guidance from teachers and elders
(Essa & Burnham, 2019). As we grow older, our brains become less elastic and it is more
difficult to learn new things. Meanwhile, children are doing an extraordinary amount of work,
and their environments in which they learn need to reflect that.
Characterizing the fourth year of life is a sense of self-confidence, independence, and
exploration. The fourth year of life sees a growing importance in peers and playing. A growing
understanding of the importance of sharing and cooperation leads to more group play that is
creative and imaginative. Five-year-olds improve their skills in group play, becoming more
elaborate and imaginative in the scenarios they act out (Marotz & Allen, 2015). They also begin
to take friendships more seriously by being more cooperative, sharing more often, and
communicating more effectively (Essa & Burnham, 2019). Quality engagement can start to be
encouraged during the fifth year, as they have begun to understand the consequences of their
actions, and are more willing to be responsible and reliable.
During the sixth year of life, many children will begin to attend kindergarten and before- or
after-school programs where they can be part of a community of other children. At six years old,
children are the most independent at this point in their lives, and they are much more capable and
willing to follow rules and standards that are set in place without needing to be monitored
constantly by adults. Children also start to consider the viewpoint of their peers, taking on a more
empathetic mindset (Essa & Burnham, 2019). Friendships with same-sex individuals become
increasingly important as they are now playing at a more complex and organized level than
before, they also tend to develop their own rules for their games (Essa & Burnham, 2019). The
15

following sections will begin to examine how the classroom or learning environment can have
positive and negative effects on the development of children, followed by a list of definitions that
will be utilized throughout this study.
IV. STUDENT ENGAGEMENT
The overall term “engagement” can be broken up into three different categories:
behavioral/social, cognitive, and emotional. Behavioral and social engagement considers the
extent to which a student aligns with behavior expectations in a classroom (Cooper, 2014). So, if
it is expected that a child raises their hand for questions, participates in group activities, shares
supplies with peers, then the degree to which the child follows those expectations is their level of
behavioral and social engagement. Cognitive engagement considers the extent to which a student
puts forth mental effort into their studies and situations (Gesualdi, 2019). This can include
situations where the student is investigating and examining new information, dealing with mental
and social challenges, etc. and how much mental effort they put forth in completing those tasks.
Emotional engagement is the degree to which a student feels positively about a class (Gesualdi,
2019). If the student feels happy, comfortable, and interested in being in the classroom and in
succeeding, then they are emotionally engaged.
We can further break down these engagement categories into positive and negative. Positive
engagement between students and their peers, teachers, and tasks is exhibited by students being
motivated, confident, and having an intent to succeed (Vitiello et al., 2012). Positive engagement
includes sharing between peers, actively working on assignments, asking the teacher meaningful
and deliberate questions, and acting positively towards other students and teachers. Negative
engagement between students and their peers, teachers, and tasks is exhibited by students having
a lack of motivation, lack of intent to succeed, conflicts, and dysregulation (Vitiello et al., 2012).
16

This type of engagement may include instances of conflicts between students and their peers or
teachers, a lack of sharing supplies, lack of motivation to complete a task, or a lack of intent to
succeed.
Being engaged within groups is important for children’s social education. It cannot be
ignored that learning to work, learn, and play within groups is essential to build social skills,
confidence, and learning opportunities through peers (Proshansky & Fabian, 2013). Working and
playing in groups gives children opportunities to develop skills on solving issues, developing
empathy, and learning to communicate their feelings. Being engaged, or actively involved, in a
task or activity helps build the child’s capabilities of focusing, which is a crucial skill for later
academic years and many careers. Part of engagement involves focused attention and the intent
to spend time on an activity. Researchers have noted that focused attention is an important aspect
for learning throughout the various stages of life (Fisher et al., 2013; Fisher et al., 2014). The
more time that people spend actively focused on a task, the more information they will learn and
take away for use later on. The classroom is a space where attention is crucial, as students are
supposed to learn a multitude of topics that will be important in their development process.
Researchers have found that children in a sparsely decorated classroom spent less time off-task,
and consequently, they learned more from their lessons, able to apply that knowledge to tests
(Fisher et al., 2013). Through the research of Fisher et al. (2013), it is clear that an overly
decorated classroom with “visual bombardment” can produce negative cognitive engagement.
